sections.heading: Title
sections.source_text: This paper, from NVIDIA Research and presented at CVPR 2023, tackles a safety-critical gap in object pose estimation: existing two-stage pipelines detect keypoints and solve for the 6D pose, but give no provable guarantee on how wrong the answer might be. The authors inject two changes into that pipeline. Conformal keypoint detection turns heuristic heatmap detections into circular or elliptical prediction sets that provably cover the true keypoints with a user-chosen probability, say ninety percent. Geometric uncertainty propagation then pushes those keypoint sets through the geometry to form a Pose Uncertainty Set, or PURSE, that covers the true pose with the same probability. From PURSE they compute an average pose by random sample averaging, and use semidefinite relaxation to bound the worst-case rotation and translation error. On the LineMOD Occlusion dataset the sets achieve valid coverage, the bounds are correct, and the average pose matches or beats strong baselines.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.source_text: Estimating an object's 6D pose from an image underlies augmented reality, autonomous driving, robotic manipulation, and space robotics. The dominant recipe is a two-stage pipeline: first detect semantic keypoints on the image, then compute the pose by minimizing reprojection error through Perspective-n-Points. These methods score well on standard benchmarks, but they hand back a single pose with no statement about how trustworthy it is. For safety-critical systems that is a serious gap, because there is no provable guarantee on the quality of the keypoints, no guarantee the optimizer found the right pose, and no formal bound on the worst-case error between the estimate and the truth.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.source_text: Why is this hard? The authors name three challenges. First, keypoints from neural networks can be arbitrarily wrong, producing outliers. Second, the second stage must reject those outliers, which is a nonconvex optimization; fast heuristics like RANSAC are widely used but cannot guarantee global optimality and often fail without notice. Third, and most fundamentally, there is no provably correct uncertainty quantification, meaning no formal worst-case error bound between the estimate and the groundtruth. Recent work could certify global optimality of the optimization, but that still does not deliver a probabilistic guarantee on the pose itself. This paper sets out to provide exactly that guarantee, end to end.

sections.heading: Method
sections.source_text: The method works in two stages. In conformal keypoint detection, a calibration set of labeled images is used to compute nonconformity scores for the heatmap detector. The authors offer two score designs: a peak design that measures the scaled distance between the true keypoint and the heatmap's most probable pixel, and a covariance design that measures a Mahalanobis distance over the top detections, giving circular and elliptical prediction sets respectively. Sorting these scores yields a threshold that guarantees each true keypoint lies in its prediction set with probability one minus epsilon. In geometric uncertainty propagation, these keypoint sets become quadratic constraints on the 6D pose, defining the Pose Uncertainty Set. Since that set is nonconvex, RANSAG samples three keypoints at a time, solves the minimal P3P problem, keeps poses inside the set, and averages them into an average pose. Finally, to bound the error, the authors maximize the distance from the average pose to the farthest pose still inside PURSE, relax this nonconvex problem into a semidefinite program, and solve it, producing certified worst-case rotation and translation bounds.

sections.heading: Key Result
sections.source_text: The results confirm the theory on all three fronts. First, the conformal prediction sets achieve valid coverage: at a target of ninety percent, the empirical coverage across objects sits right around ninety percent, and it concentrates more tightly as the calibration set grows. Second, the worst-case error bounds are correct: in the scatter plots comparing the certified bound against the actual error, every case where PURSE covers the true pose stays below the diagonal, meaning the bound is never violated when the guarantee holds. Third, the average pose is accurate: judged by the two-dimensional projection metric, it achieves significantly higher success rates than prior methods when using groundtruth bounding boxes, and comparable rates when using Faster-RCNN detections.

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.source_text: The lasting message is that you can turn a standard two-stage pose estimator into one that tells you how wrong it might be, with a real statistical guarantee, and pay little to nothing in accuracy. Conformal prediction supplies coverage guarantees on the keypoints, geometry propagates those guarantees to the pose as the Pose Uncertainty Set, and semidefinite relaxation converts the set into concrete worst-case error bounds. Because it wraps any heatmap-based keypoint detector, the approach is broadly applicable, and it opens a path toward provably correct perception for other geometric vision problems where safety matters.
